lines.text: For more than three thousand years people have asked what is true, what is good and how to live. These are the faiths and thinkers who answered.
It begins in northern India with the Rigveda, more than a thousand hymns kept alive by memory for centuries before anyone wrote them down.
From those roots grew Hinduism, a family of traditions with many gods and shared ideas of duty, rebirth and release, still the faith of most of India.
Its early form, the Vedic religion, centred on fire sacrifices to gods such as Indra and Agni, and slowly gave way to later Hindu practice.
Far to the west, the Bible tells of Moses, who led the Israelites out of Egypt and received the law at Sinai. Whether he lived is still debated.
In Iran, Zoroastrianism taught of a great struggle between truth and falsehood under the god Ahura Mazda. It became the faith of Persian empires.
Meanwhile Judaism took shape around one God, a covenant and the Torah. From this root, Christianity and Islam would one day grow.
Its sacred writings, gathered over many centuries by many hands, became the Bible, in time the most translated and most printed book on Earth.
In the Greek city of Miletus, Thales looked for natural causes instead of stories about gods, and so is often called the first Western philosopher.
Back in India, Jainism asked its followers to harm no living thing, to tell the truth and to let go, the path its teachers say frees the soul.
In China, tradition credits the sage Laozi with the Tao Te Ching. No one is sure he lived, but his name became the heart of Daoism.
Pythagoras of Samos founded a community in southern Italy that mixed numbers, music and religion. A famous theorem still carries his name.
In the foothills of the Himalaya, a prince left his palace to seek the end of suffering. As the Buddha, he taught a path that would cross all of Asia.
At almost the same time Confucius taught in China about duty, family, learning and good government. His students wrote down his sayings in the Analects.
Confucianism grew from those lessons, and for over two thousand years it shaped schools, families and governments across East Asia.
Buddhism spread out from northern India along roads and rivers, dividing into schools such as Theravada and Mahayana as it went.
Indian storytellers sang the Ramayana, in which Prince Rama and the monkey Hanuman rescue Sita from the demon king, a tale still danced across Asia.
In Athens, Socrates questioned everyone he met about justice and virtue. He wrote nothing, and a jury of his own city sentenced him to death.
His student Plato kept that voice alive in dialogues like the Republic, and founded the Academy to ask how a just city should be run.
India's other great epic, the Mahabharata, told of a war between two branches of one royal family, in about a hundred thousand verses.
In China, Taoism urged people to live in harmony with the Tao, the hidden way of nature, and later became a religion of temples and priests.
Its founding book, the Tao Te Ching, is only eighty-one short chapters, yet it is among the most translated texts ever written.
Aristotle studied under Plato, tutored Alexander the Great and wrote on almost everything, from logic and ethics to animals. Europe and Islam read him for centuries.
Mencius carried Confucian thought further, arguing that people are born inclined to goodness and that a ruler must care for his people.
Zhuangzi answered with stories and jokes about freedom, change and how little we really know, a playful voice in the Taoist tradition.
In a garden in Athens, Epicurus taught that a good life is a calm one, free of fear and pain, found in friendship and simple pleasures.
Nearby, under a painted porch, Zeno of Cyprus founded Stoicism, teaching that virtue and self-control matter more than wealth or luck.
Then, in Roman Judea, a Jewish teacher from Galilee preached of love and the kingdom of God. Jesus was crucified, and his followers spread his message.
From a small Jewish group, Christianity spread through the Roman Empire and became, in time, the largest religion in the world.
Led by the bishop of Rome, the Catholic Church traces itself back to the apostles, and grew into the largest of the Christian churches.
In the east, the Orthodox churches of Greece, Russia and beyond share the same roots. The two halves formally parted ways in 1054.
A Roman emperor, Marcus Aurelius, lived by Stoic ideas while defending his borders. His private notes, the Meditations, are still read today.
In India, the Buddhist thinker Nagarjuna taught a middle way, arguing that nothing has a fixed nature of its own.
In North Africa, Bishop Augustine joined Christian faith with Greek ideas in his Confessions and City of God, shaping the Western Church for centuries.
In Mecca, around the year 570, Muhammad was born. Muslims believe God revealed the Quran to him, and by his death most of Arabia followed his message.
In Japan, people honoured the kami, the spirits of nature and of ancestors, in a faith called Shinto that grew up alongside Buddhism.
Islam taught submission to one God, lived out through the Five Pillars. Within a century it reached from Spain to India.
Its holy book, the Quran, was revealed over some twenty-three years, Muslims believe. Recited in Arabic worldwide, it also shaped the Arabic language.
When Muhammad died in 632, the community divided. Shia Muslims held that leadership belonged to his cousin and son-in-law Ali and his line.
Sunni Muslims accepted the chosen caliphs instead, and today about nine in every ten Muslims are Sunni.
In India, the monk Adi Shankara taught that the self and ultimate reality are one, and founded monasteries across the land.
In Persia, Avicenna was both doctor and philosopher. His Canon of Medicine was a standard textbook in Islamic lands and Europe for centuries.
In Song China, Confucian thought was reborn with new ideas about the universe and the self, a revival called Neo-Confucianism.
Al-Ghazali challenged the philosophers and wrote on law, theology and Sufism, becoming one of the most read thinkers in Islamic history.
In Cordoba, the judge Averroes wrote careful commentaries on Aristotle. Translated into Latin, they were studied closely in medieval Europe.
Zhu Xi gave Confucian teaching its systematic form and chose the Four Books, which became the basis of China's state examinations for centuries.
Also born in Cordoba, Maimonides became a court physician in Egypt, organised Jewish law and tried to reconcile faith with Aristotle.
Thomas Aquinas did the same for Christianity, weaving Aristotle into Church teaching in his great Summa Theologiae.
In Tunis, Ibn Khaldun asked why societies and states rise and fall. His Muqaddimah is seen as an early work of sociology and economics.
In the Punjab, Guru Nanak taught one God, honest work, sharing and the equality of all people, and his hymns became scripture.
In Florence, Machiavelli wrote The Prince, showing how rulers really win and keep power, not how they ought to. His name became a byword.
In Ming China, Wang Yangming taught that knowing and doing cannot be separated, and that moral understanding lies within the mind.
In Germany, the monk Martin Luther challenged the sale of indulgences in 1517, and translated the Bible into German for ordinary people.
Meanwhile Sikhism took shape under Guru Nanak and the nine gurus after him, gathering its people in gurdwaras for worship and shared meals.
Luther's challenge became the Reformation, splitting Western Christianity in two and bringing more than a century of religious wars.
The new Protestant churches rejected the Pope's authority and put the Bible first, a change that reshaped much of Europe.
In England, Francis Bacon argued that knowledge of nature should be built from observation and experiment, inspiring the founders of the Royal Society.
Thomas Hobbes warned in Leviathan that without strong government, life would be a war of all against all, so people agree to obey for safety.
In France, Descartes tried to rebuild knowledge on certainty itself, starting from one idea: I think, therefore I am.
John Locke said the mind begins blank, and that people have natural rights to life, liberty and property, ideas that later fired two revolutions.
In Amsterdam, Baruch Spinoza argued that God and nature are one, and was expelled by his own Jewish community for it.
In Haiti, enslaved Africans blended their traditions with Catholic elements into Vodou, honouring spirits called lwa with drums, song and dance.
In Scotland, David Hume argued that all knowledge comes from experience, and that logic alone cannot prove cause and effect.
From Geneva, Rousseau wrote The Social Contract, holding that a government's power comes from the people. The French Revolution took note.
In Konigsberg, Immanuel Kant argued that the mind shapes how we experience the world and that duty follows from reason, a turning point in philosophy.
In 1792 Mary Wollstonecraft argued that women deserve the same education as men, an early and powerful voice for women's rights.
Hegel saw history as ideas unfolding through conflict and resolution, a difficult vision that shaped the thinkers who came after him.
John Stuart Mill defended individual freedom in On Liberty, argued that right actions bring the most happiness, and called for votes for women.
In Denmark, Soren Kierkegaard wrote of anxiety, choice and faith, insisting each person must find meaning by living. Many call him the first existentialist.
Karl Marx argued that history is driven by struggles between classes. His Communist Manifesto and Das Kapital went on to shape politics worldwide.
In America in 1830, Joseph Smith published the Book of Mormon, beginning the Latter Day Saint movement, today centred in Salt Lake City.
Friedrich Nietzsche questioned morality and religion, declared that God is dead, and urged people to create their own values.
In 1893 the Indian monk Swami Vivekananda spoke in Chicago at a world parliament of religions, bringing Hindu thought to Western audiences.
In Persia, Baha'u'llah founded the Baha'i Faith, teaching that all great religions come from one God and that humanity is one family.
Mahatma Gandhi turned faith into nonviolent protest, leading India's struggle against British rule. He was killed months after independence.
At Cambridge, Ludwig Wittgenstein studied how language meets the world, and then changed his mind radically between his two great books.
In the early 1900s, Pentecostalism rose in the United States with speaking in tongues, healing and lively worship, and grew quickly worldwide.
In Paris, Jean-Paul Sartre argued that we have no fixed nature and must make ourselves through our choices. He turned down a Nobel Prize.
Hannah Arendt fled the Nazis and wrote about totalitarianism and responsibility, coining the phrase the banality of evil.
In 1949 Simone de Beauvoir published The Second Sex, arguing that one is not born a woman but becomes one, a foundation of modern feminism.
In America, John Rawls asked what rules we would choose for society if we did not know our own place in it.
Michel Foucault studied how prisons, hospitals and schools shape people, and how power works through knowledge.
Noam Chomsky argued that humans are born ready for grammar, and became one of the best-known critics of American power.
In Germany, Jurgen Habermas argued that democracy lives on free and open public debate, guided by reason.
In 1930s Jamaica, Rastafari arose, honouring Haile Selassie of Ethiopia and looking to Africa as a spiritual home, carried worldwide by reggae.
Tibet's Dalai Lama fled to India in 1959 and led a government in exile, teaching compassion worldwide and winning the Nobel Peace Prize.
Pope Francis, the first pope from the Americas, spoke for the poor, for migrants and for the planet, until his death in 2025.
Peter Singer's Animal Liberation launched the modern animal rights movement, and he helped found effective altruism.
In May 2025 the cardinals chose Robert Prevost, who became Pope Leo the fourteenth, the first pope born in the United States.
And looking back to the sixties, the Second Vatican Council brought the Mass into local languages and opened the Church to other faiths.
The questions are as old as the Vedas, and every generation still answers them anew.
